summary.headline: Meta's new non-voting Class C stock and founder dividend ladder separate control from economics, while a $9.89 billion legal charge cut Q3 operating income 37% and capex pushed free cash flow to negative $2.12 billion.

bullets.label: Non-voting class created
bullets.detail: Stockholders approved a restated charter creating publicly listed non-voting Class C common stock effective January 19, 2027, with a one-for-one Class C stock dividend on each Class A and Class B share. The recital states the company expects to issue Class C to raise capital, fund acquisitions and compensate employees, so future dilution no longer requires giving up founder voting power. The dividend record date, share count and listing mechanics were not disclosed in the exhibit.

bullets.label: Open-ended founder dilution
bullets.detail: Under the Founder Alignment Agreement the board must declare an Additional Dividend of one Class C share for every outstanding Class A, Class B and Class C share once the 30-day VWAP reaches successive doublings of the $580.60 September 10, 2026 baseline (2x, 4x, 8x and so on) with at least a 10% annualized shareholder return. The agreement sets no time limit, permits separate dividends for multiple doubling events on the same date, and expressly makes no price adjustment for equity issued for AI-infrastructure investment. No cap on cumulative issuance was disclosed.

bullets.label: Founder sales stapled
bullets.detail: Only 20% of the Class C shares Zuckerberg's holder group receives in the stock dividend are freely saleable; the other 80% are stapled and release at 2.5% per quarter over up to 32 qualifying quarters, conditioned on continued full-time service, with each sale of stapled shares requiring an offsetting Class A/B sale or conversion. A breach triggers automatic Class B-to-Class A conversion rather than damages. This paces potential insider supply but leaves voting control intact until voting stock is sold or converted.

bullets.label: Legal charge hits Q3 profit
bullets.detail: Third quarter 2026 revenue was $64.60 billion, up 26% year-over-year, but general and administrative expense rose to $14.86 billion from $3.51 billion on the $9.89 billion state attorneys general charge, cutting operating income to $12.99 billion (down 37% year-over-year) and operating margin to 20% from 40%. Excluding the charge, operating income would have been $22.88 billion and diluted EPS $7.40 versus $3.83 reported. The August 2026 agreement provides for payments of up to approximately $18.59 billion, leaving roughly $8.7 billion uncharged, and youth-related U.S. trials remain scheduled.

bullets.label: Buybacks halted, debt raised
bullets.detail: There were no Class A repurchases in the third quarter or first nine months of 2026 versus $26.25 billion in the prior-year nine months, while net long-term debt proceeds of $24.91 billion lifted long-term debt to $80.92 billion from $58.74 billion at December 31, 2025. Capital expenditures including finance leases of $34.91 billion turned third quarter free cash flow negative $2.12 billion from positive $10.63 billion a year earlier, even with operating cash flow of $32.79 billion. Management guides 2026 capital expenditures of $135-145 billion, so the funding mix remains debt- and balance-sheet-dependent.

summary.analystView: The governance change is the more durable signal: Class C lets Meta fund AI infrastructure and acquisitions with equity while the founder's voting position is preserved, and the doubling-linked dividends add a shareholder-return-contingent claim on the equity base. Next checks are whether those dividends are recorded as stock dividends or compensation expense, the record date and share count of the initial dividend, and whether capex guidance keeps fourth quarter free cash flow negative.

summary.headline: Meta's Q2 2026 revenue rose 28%, but a $2.40 billion legal charge and $1.18 billion severance lifted costs 55%, cutting operating income 8% and free cash flow to $784 million.

bullets.label: Costs outrun revenue on charges
bullets.detail: Total costs and expenses rose 55% year-over-year to $42.03 billion in Q2 2026 from $27.08 billion, including $2.40 billion of legal-proceeding charges and $1.18 billion of severance tied to the May 2026 headcount reduction, while revenue grew 28%. Operating income fell 8% year-over-year to $18.78 billion and operating margin dropped to 31% from 43%. The company does not disclose the cost growth rate excluding the $3.58 billion of charges, so whether the restructuring savings are durable or offset by AI-related hiring remains unverified.

bullets.label: Free cash flow nearly eliminated
bullets.detail: Operating cash flow was $31.86 billion versus $25.56 billion a year earlier, but capital expenditures including finance-lease principal reached $31.08 billion (versus purchases of property and equipment of $16.54 billion plus $0.47 billion of finance-lease principal in Q2 2025), leaving free cash flow of $784 million against $8.55 billion. First-half free cash flow was $13.17 billion versus $18.88 billion. Only about 2.5% of quarterly operating cash flow converted to discretionary cash, a structural change in cash conversion rather than a one-quarter timing item.

bullets.label: Debt funds capex as buybacks stop
bullets.detail: Meta raised $24.91 billion of net long-term debt in Q2 2026, lifting long-term debt to $83.66 billion at June 30, 2026 from $58.74 billion at December 31, 2025. There were no Class A repurchases in either 2026 period, versus $10.17 billion in Q2 2025 and $22.92 billion in first-half 2025, while dividends of $1.35 billion continued. Cash, cash equivalents and marketable securities were $90.26 billion, so liquidity is ample, but shareholder returns are now subordinate to debt-funded infrastructure spending; terms and maturities of the new debt are not disclosed in the release.

bullets.label: Outlook: higher expense and tax
bullets.detail: Full-year 2026 total expenses are guided to $165-169 billion, with the low end raised to absorb the $2.4 billion legal charge, and the expected tax rate for remaining quarters rose to 15-17% from 13-16%. 2026 capital expenditures including finance-lease principal were narrowed to $130-145 billion from $125-145 billion, effectively lifting the midpoint. Q3 2026 revenue is guided to $61-64 billion with an approximately 1% foreign-exchange headwind, and management still expects 2026 operating income above 2025.

bullets.label: Youth litigation loss warning
bullets.detail: Management stated that youth-related trials scheduled in the U.S. this year "may ultimately result in a material loss," a risk incremental to the $2.40 billion of legal charges already booked in Q2 2026. No loss range, timing or probable-outcome estimate is provided, so the potential cash and earnings impact cannot be sized from this release. This makes the legal overhang live and recurring rather than a one-time second-quarter item, and it sits alongside the newly committed capex and debt plans.

summary.analystView: Earnings are being converted into AI infrastructure rather than shareholder cash: operating income fell 8% year-over-year while capex ran at $31.08 billion and repurchases stopped, so returns now depend on monetizing that capacity before depreciation and legal costs compound. The next checks are Q3 expense growth excluding the $3.58 billion of charges, disclosure on commitments behind the $130-145 billion capex range, and any quantified youth-litigation loss estimate.

summary.headline: Meta shareholders re-elected all 12 directors and ratified EY, while concentrated withheld votes hit Elkann and Alford and about a quarter backed pay and dual-class reviews.

bullets.label: Director opposition concentrated
bullets.detail: All twelve nominees were elected, but John Elkann received 4,110,029,835 votes for and 858,647,251 withheld, or about 17.3% withheld of votes cast for and withheld, while Peggy Alford had 677,536,447 withheld, or about 13.6%; Arnold and Collison were each near 1.0%. The concentration suggests targeted shareholder concern rather than a broad rejection of the board, but the exhibit gives no reason for the opposition. The next check is the company’s engagement disclosure and whether the withheld vote persists next year.

bullets.label: Annual pay vote rejected
bullets.detail: A shareholder proposal to move to annual advisory votes on executive pay failed, with 1,347,044,885 for, 3,615,585,963 against and 6,046,238 abstentions, or about 27.1% support of votes cast excluding broker non-votes. That minority is large enough to signal compensation-oversight pressure even though the proposal did not pass. The exhibit does not state the current say-on-pay frequency; the proxy statement is the next check.

bullets.label: Control proposals rejected
bullets.detail: A dual-class review proposal failed with 1,312,681,056 for and 3,647,675,248 against, about 26.4% support, and a per-share-class voting disclosure proposal failed with 998,846,306 for and 3,963,963,497 against, about 20.1% support, in each case of votes cast excluding broker non-votes. The Class B shares carry ten votes each versus one for Class A, so the support level points to governance-transparency concerns even though the structure was unchanged. No management commitment to additional class-level disclosure was disclosed.

bullets.label: Auditor ratified
bullets.detail: Shareholders ratified Ernst & Young LLP as independent registered public accounting firm for fiscal 2026 with 5,148,139,817 for, 29,583,257 against and 3,810,576 abstentions, and there were no broker non-votes. The margin is routine and removes auditor ratification as a governance flashpoint. The filing discloses no change in auditor or audit-related terms.

bullets.label: Other proposals fail broadly
bullets.detail: The remaining shareholder proposals, covering AI data usage oversight, human rights due diligence, antisemitism and hate, climate commitments, child safety in executive compensation, generative-AI data protection and H-1B visa risks, all failed; support ranged from about 0.2% to 10.1% of votes cast excluding broker non-votes. The AI data usage proposal drew the high end at 503,719,383 for, while the H-1B proposal drew 11,628,532 for. None of these outcomes changes company policy directly, but the low-to-moderate support indicates limited shareholder backing for the requested reports.

summary.analystView: The meeting is a governance signal rather than a financial event: the board is unchanged and all shareholder proposals failed, but targeted director opposition and roughly one-fifth to one-quarter support for pay and control transparency may increase engagement pressure. The next verification is whether the 2027 proxy shows lower withheld votes or any voluntary change in say-on-pay frequency, dual-class disclosure or board composition; no earnings, cash flow or balance-sheet effect is disclosed.

summary.headline: Meta priced $25B of senior notes across six tranches, adding long-dated fixed debt and a roughly $1.43B annual interest cost based on stated coupons.

bullets.label: Six-tranche $25B raise
bullets.detail: Meta priced $25.0B aggregate principal across six senior-note tranches: $3.0B 4.550% due 2031, $2.0B 4.875% due 2033, $6.0B 5.250% due 2036, $4.0B 6.200% due 2046, $6.0B 6.300% due 2056 and $4.0B 6.450% due 2066. The pricing adds long-dated fixed-rate obligations and extends the maturity ladder, but the excerpt does not state use of proceeds, so the effect on leverage and cash depends on whether proceeds fund capex, repay debt or are held as cash.

bullets.label: Interest cost and coupon curve
bullets.detail: Based on the stated principal amounts and coupons, the six tranches carry about $1.43B of annual interest cost, equivalent to a weighted-average coupon near 5.73%. The 2066 notes at 6.450% price 190 bp above the 2031 notes at 4.550%, showing a steep term premium for 40-year money. That fixes a long-run cost of debt, but the excerpt does not give the all-in weighted-average maturity or state whether any existing lower-coupon debt is refinanced.

bullets.label: Maturity mix
bullets.detail: Only $5.0B of the $25.0B principal matures in 2031-2033, while $10.0B matures in 2056-2066 and $10.0B in 2036-2046. The long-dated structure reduces near-term refinancing pressure but commits Meta to fixed coupons for decades and adds duration risk if rates rise further. The exhibit does not disclose the post-offering maturity profile or any sinking-fund or call features.

bullets.label: Scale versus balance sheet
bullets.detail: The $25.0B principal equals about 43% of the $58.748B long-term debt reported at 2026-03-31 (GAAP quarter-end) and is $1.574B larger than the $23.426B cash balance at the same date. Long-term debt had already risen to $58.748B at 2026-03-31 from $28.834B at 2025-09-30 (GAAP quarter-end), so the new raise would extend a sharp debt build. Actual leverage and interest coverage require pro forma debt and EBITDA, which the excerpt does not provide.

bullets.label: Reopening risk
bullets.detail: Each series is described as "initially limited" to its stated principal and may be increased under the indenture, so the $25.0B headline is not a contractual ceiling for this debt stack.
